# The fixture corpus

`docs/DIAGNOSTIC_PLAN.md` Phase 28, field 13:

> A fixture corpus of at least four real projects — and **at least two the
> author did not write**, in stacks the author does not control. This is a
> hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: it is the only defence against
> building an extractor that only works on FastAPI because
> `demo-services/` is FastAPI.

Four projects, and the two that matter most are the ones nobody here wrote.

| Fixture | Stack | Written by | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fastapi-orders/` | FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic | this repo | The home stack. Committed OpenAPI document, `.env.example`, an Alembic chain with a branch, a compose file. |
| `react-web/` | React, TypeScript, Vite | this repo | The other half of "a Python+React repository" (acceptance criterion 1): client call sites and a `package.json` full of scoped packages. |
| `indexed-shop/` | Alembic | this repo | Phase 37 part 1: one migration with a primary key and one index, and a `culprit.yaml` reaching a database through `dsn_env`. `TestIndexesDeclaredAndLive` builds the same schema in a real Postgres and drops and adds indexes by hand. |
| `third-party/flask-tutorial/` | **Flask**, blueprints, `sqlite3` | **Pallets** | Flask, not FastAPI. Blueprints with prefixes, `<int:id>` converters, an `app.config.from_mapping` rather than `os.environ`, and `SECRET_KEY` set to a literal in source. |
| `third-party/express-route-separation/` | **Express**, EJS | **TJ Holowaychuk / Express** | Node, not Python. Routes registered across four modules against one `app`, `:id` parameters, and a `package.json` this repo did not write. |

## Why third-party fixtures are non-negotiable

An extractor tested only against code written alongside it passes because
both sides share the same assumptions. The Flask fixture immediately
proved the point: it configures itself through `app.config.from_mapping`
and never touches `os.environ`, so the config-key reader — which works
perfectly on this repo's own services — finds nothing in it. That is a
real limitation of the extractor, and it is only visible because the
fixture was not written to suit it.

## Provenance and licences

Both third-party fixtures are vendored **unmodified**, at a pinned
upstream version, with their own licence files kept alongside them.

- `third-party/flask-tutorial/` — [pallets/flask](https://github.com/pallets/flask)
  `examples/tutorial` at tag **3.1.0**. BSD-3-Clause; see its `LICENSE.txt`.
- `third-party/express-route-separation/` — [expressjs/express](https://github.com/expressjs/express)
  `examples/route-separation` at tag **4.21.2**. MIT; see its `LICENSE`.

Do not edit them. Their value is that they are exactly what somebody else
shipped — an edit to make a test pass turns a third-party fixture back
into one of ours, silently.

## Golden files

`golden/<fixture>.json` is the expected `culprit intent --format json`
output. They are generated by `just cli-golden-update` and asserted by
`cli/internal/extract/golden_test.go`.

Golden runs pass `--no-plugins` and pin the clock. Both are deliberate:
plugins would make the Go test depend on a Python and a Node toolchain
being installed, and an unpinned clock changes `captured_at` and the
derived capture id on every run. What the golden files pin is the
**artefact readers** — the part that must work with nothing installed
(acceptance criterion 4). The plugins have their own tests, in their own
languages, against these same fixtures.
